scenes.say: A base pointer, a missing keyword, and a thousand bytes gone for good. By the end, you'll draw the vtable behind a virtual call, and name the five special functions.
Today you will do three things. Tell overloading from overriding, and plug a leak. Know the rule of three, five, zero. And draw the vtable, and fix the diamond.
lines: Draw the vtable; fix the diamond

scenes.title: Overloading or overriding?
scenes.statement: Two similar words, two different mechanisms. Say which is chosen at compile time and which at runtime.
scenes.say: Print of forty two, and draw called through a base reference. Interviewers love this pair, because the words sound alike.

scenes.head: Overloading: same name, new parameters
scenes.say: Overloading: one name, several parameter lists, in one scope. The compiler matches argument types at compile time. Forty two picks int. Three point one four picks double. But you cannot overload on the return type alone.

scenes.head: Overriding: replace a virtual
scenes.say: Overriding: a derived class replaces a base virtual, same signature. Here b is a Base reference, but the object is a Derived. So Derived's draw runs, decided at runtime. Always write override.
Your turn. Base has f of int and f of double. Derived declares only f of int. We call d dot f with two point five. Which version runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Derived declares only `f(int)`. What does `d.f(2.5)` call?

scenes.head: The trap: a derived name hides base overloads
scenes.say: Derived f of int. A derived f hides every base f, including the double one. So two point five quietly converts to int, and Derived's version runs. The fix is a using declaration, using Base f, which brings the base overloads back.

scenes.head: Overloading versus overriding
scenes.say: Scope? One scope, versus base and derived. Signature? Differs, versus matches. When? Compile time, versus runtime. Keyword? None, versus override. So overloading is compile time polymorphism, overriding is runtime.

scenes.title: Why a virtual destructor?
scenes.statement: Delete a Derived object through a Base pointer. The Derived owns a 1 KB buffer. Does the buffer get freed?

example.input: Base* p = new Derived; delete p;

scenes.say: Picture a Derived holding one kilobyte, deleted through a Base pointer. Is the buffer freed?

scenes.head: delete through a base pointer
scenes.say: P is a Base pointer to a Derived object. The Derived part owns a one kilobyte heap buffer. Delete p, with no virtual destructor. Only Base's destructor runs. Derived's never does, so the buffer leaks.
Your turn. Now we make Base's destructor virtual. Both destructors print their name. What gets printed when we delete p? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The fix: one keyword
scenes.say: Derived first, then Base. The destructor is virtual, so delete looks up the real type at runtime. Derived's destructor runs first, then Base's: the reverse of construction. A unique pointer to Base needs this too.

scenes.head: The rule, and two follow-ups
scenes.say: The rule: a polymorphic base gets a public virtual destructor. Or make it protected and non virtual, so deleting through the base won't compile. A shared pointer remembers the real type, but don't rely on that.

scenes.title: What if a constructor throws?
scenes.statement: A Car builds an engine and wheels, then its constructor throws. Which destructors run, and in what order?
scenes.say: A Car builds its engine, then its wheels, then throws. Which destructors run?
Your turn. Car has two Part members, and a destructor that prints ~Car. The constructor body throws. Does ~Car run? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Built members are destroyed, Car is not
scenes.say: No. The object never finished construction, so its lifetime never began. Nothing for ~Car to destroy. Members already built are destroyed in reverse. Each Part prints plus when built, minus when destroyed: plus engine, plus wheels, minus wheels, minus engine.

scenes.head: The trap: raw resources leak
scenes.say: Raw resources in constructors are dangerous. On the left, new allocates, then connect throws. The destructor never runs, so the buffer leaks. On the right, a vector member is fully built, so it is destroyed. That is R A I I.

panels.label: leaks
safe

scenes.head: Two more facts interviewers like
scenes.say: Two more facts. A throwing constructor inside new frees the memory, and the pointer is never assigned. A function try block can catch, but then rethrows. And throwing is how a constructor reports failure.
rows: throw: it has no return value

scenes.title: Copy constructor or copy assignment?
scenes.statement: Three lines copy one T into another. Which of them call the copy constructor, and which call copy assignment?

example.input: T b = a;  T c(a);  c = b;

scenes.say: Three lines: T b equals a, T c of a, and c equals b. Which one is assignment?
Your turn. Ask one question: does the object on the left already exist? Now, T b equals a. Which function runs? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Which one runs?
scenes.say: The copy constructor. B is created right there, even with an equals sign. Same for c of a. Only c equals b, where c already exists, calls copy assignment. Passing or returning by value also uses the copy constructor.

output.text:
copy ctor
copy ctor
copy assign

scenes.head: Why assignment has more work
scenes.say: Assignment is harder, because the target already owns memory. First, guard against self assignment. Then make a fresh copy, delete the old block, and adopt the new one. Return star this, so assignments chain. A copy constructor needs none of this.

scenes.title: Rule of three, five, zero
scenes.statement: A class owns heap memory and frees it in its destructor. Copy it, and the program crashes. Why, and what do you write?
scenes.say: A Buffer owns an array and frees it in its destructor. We copy it, and at the end of main the program dies. Why?

scenes.head: The bug: default copy copies the pointer
scenes.say: Buffer a owns an array of three. Default copy copies the pointer, so b gets the same one. At the end, b frees the array. Then a deletes it again. A double delete: undefined behavior.

scenes.head: Rule of three, then five
scenes.say: The rule of three: write one of destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment, and you need all three, with deep copies. Rule of five adds a move constructor and move assignment, which steal the pointer.
Your turn. A class declares a destructor and a copy constructor, but no move. We write S b equals move of a. Which function runs? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `S` declares `~S()` and a copy ctor, no move. `S b = std::move(a);` runs...

scenes.head: Declare one, lose the moves
scenes.say: The copy constructor. Once you declare a destructor, the compiler stops generating moves, so your moves silently become copies. Even better: the rule of zero. Hold the resource in a member, and write none.

scenes.head: Rule of zero: let members own it
scenes.say: In the rule of zero, you write none. A vector member copies deeply and moves cheaply, and the compiler's own copies call the vector's. Prefer zero. Use five only to own a resource.

scenes.title: The diamond problem
scenes.statement: A Bat is a Mammal and a Bird, and both are Animals. How many Animals does a Bat hold, and what does b.id mean?
scenes.say: A Bat is a Mammal and a Bird, and both are Animals. How many Animals sit inside one Bat?

scenes.head: Inside a Bat
scenes.say: With ordinary inheritance, each path brings its own base. Mammal holds an Animal. Bird holds another. So one Bat contains two Animals, each with its own id, and b dot id is ambiguous. Now inherit virtually. Both paths share one Animal, and b dot id just works.
Your turn. Now the bases are virtual. Mammal passes id one to Animal. Bird passes two. Bat's own constructor passes three. What is b dot id? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Virtual bases. Mammal passes 1, Bird 2, Bat 3. What is `b.id`?

scenes.head: Who constructs the shared base?
scenes.say: Three. With a virtual base, the most derived class constructs it directly, here Bat. The middle classes' calls to Animal are ignored. If Bat didn't call an Animal constructor, Animal would need a default one.

scenes.title: How does virtual dispatch work?
scenes.statement: A call through a base pointer lands on the derived function. What data structure makes that happen, and what does it cost?

example.output: vptr to vtable, then slot zero

scenes.say: s points at a Circle, and we call area. The compiler can't see the type, yet the right function runs. How?

scenes.head: One hidden pointer, one table per class
scenes.say: Each class with virtual functions gets one v table: an array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function. Circle overrides area, so its slot holds Circle's area. Draw isn't overridden, so that slot still points to Shape's. Every Circle object carries a hidden v pointer to this table, set by its constructor.

scenes.head: What s->area() compiles to
scenes.say: What does s arrow area compile to? Three steps. First, load the v pointer from the object. Second, read slot zero, because area is always slot zero. Third, call through it. Whatever the type, its own table finds the override.
Your turn. Plain has one int. Virtual has one int and one virtual function. On a typical sixty four bit build, how many bytes is Virtual? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `struct Virtual { int x; virtual void f() {} };` `sizeof` on 64-bit?

scenes.head: The costs
scenes.say: Sixteen. Four bytes of int, an eight byte v pointer, and padding. Tables are shared, but every object carries a pointer. Each call is an extra hop, usually not inlined. In a base constructor, the v pointer still points to the base table.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Overloading versus overriding? Overloading: same name, different parameters, chosen at compile time. Overriding: a derived class replaces a base virtual, chosen at runtime. Trap? Name hiding: fix with using.
rows: same name, new parameters: compile time

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why a virtual destructor? Else the derived destructor is skipped. What goes wrong? Undefined behavior, and leaked resources. Rule? A public virtual destructor, or a protected one.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: A constructor throws? The object never existed, so no destructor runs. Cleaned up? Built members, in reverse. And? Use R A I I members, and new frees its memory.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Constructor versus assignment? New object versus existing. T b equals a is construction. Assignment must free old state, and survive self assignment. Rule of three, five, zero? Destructor, copy, assign. Add moves. Or write none.
rows: new object vs existing; `T b = a` is ctor

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: The diamond problem? One base through two paths means two copies, and ambiguous names. Fix? Virtual inheritance: one shared base. Who constructs it? The most derived class.
rows: same base via two paths: two copies

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Vtables and vptrs? One table of function pointers per class, one hidden pointer per object. A virtual call? Load the vptr, pick a fixed slot, call. Cost? Eight bytes per object, one hop.
rows: per-class table; hidden pointer per object

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Try these three. LeetCode two oh six, reverse linked list, is pointer ownership. LeetCode one thirty eight, copy list with random pointer, is a deep copy. LeetCode one forty six, LRU cache, owns and frees nodes.
rows: LeetCode 138 · Copy List with Random Pointer

scenes.say: So say this. Virtual calls go vptr to vtable to slot. A polymorphic base needs a virtual destructor. And a class that owns a resource needs the rule of five, or better, the rule of zero.
lines: vptr, vtable, slot: that is a virtual call.
Own a resource: rule of five, or zero.
